title.title: In-class Assignment & Discussion
title.subtitle: Pick a real-world problem, debate it in small groups, and argue — in one page — whether it deserves a blockchain.

brief.heading: The assignment at a glance
brief.subtitle: A consulting exercise, not a coding one. Your job is to think clearly about a real problem and give an honest recommendation.

stats.label: Weight
stats.note: one of the course's two in-class assignments

flow.desc: Use a starter from the next slide or bring a problem from your own work or studies.
Work through the three parts. Run the blockchain lens. Disagree — then write down why.
One sentence per part. The class pushes back; you refine.
PDF, one page, group names at the top. Your instructor confirms the exact deadline.

brief.mindsetBody: you are the consultant a company hired to tell them whether blockchain is worth it. "No, and here is why" is a perfectly good answer — if it is well argued.

parts.heading: Exactly three parts — nothing else
parts.subtitle: A reader with five minutes should get the problem, the proposal, and an honest verdict. Headings in the report must match these three.

items.title: Problem statement
items.lead: What is broken today, for whom, and why?
prompts: Who are the actors — and which of them do the others have to trust?
Where exactly is the friction: time, cost, fraud, disputes, opacity?
How is it handled today, and what does that cost (money, days, errors)?
One concrete scenario beats three abstract ones.

items.title: Proposed solution
items.lead: What would a smart-contract-based design do — in plain language?
prompts: What triggers the contract, and what does it do when triggered?
What lives on-chain (ownership, votes, hashes) and what stays off-chain (documents, personal data)?
Who operates it: a company, a consortium, a DAO? Public or permissioned chain?
Which course examples is it closest to — and how does it differ?

items.title: Pros & cons of using a blockchain
items.lead: Would this actually be better than a well-run database?
prompts: At least two genuine advantages and two genuine disadvantages.
Cost, privacy, governance, legal recognition, user experience — pick the ones that bite here.
What would the non-blockchain alternative look like, and why is it worse (or better)?
End with a verdict: ✅ smart contract · ⚠️ hybrid · ❌ database — in one sentence.

parts.footer: Diagrams count toward the page. Appendices do not exist. If it doesn't fit on one page, it isn't sharp enough yet.

problemBank.heading: Pick a problem — or bring your own
problemBank.subtitle: Click a card to see the actors, the friction, one blockchain angle and one honest alternative. Use them as a springboard, not an answer key.
problemBank.selectPrompt: Select a problem to see the starter notes
problemBank.ownBody: any problem where several parties exchange value or records and at least one of them is not fully trusted. Your workplace, your sports club, your student association — all fair game.

items.title: Diploma verification
items.friction: Employers e-mail registrars and wait days; fake diplomas are a multi-billion-dollar market; students don't control their own record.
items.angle: The university anchors a hash of each diploma on-chain; the graduate holds the credential; anyone verifies in seconds (MIT Blockcerts, Section 3).
items.alternative: A national verification API run by the ministry of education — cheaper, but it makes the ministry the single point of trust and failure.

items.title: Concert ticket scalping
items.actors: Artist · promoter · ticketing platform · fans · resellers
items.friction: Bots buy out drops in seconds; resale prices explode; the artist earns nothing on resale; fakes are common at the door.
items.angle: Tickets as NFTs with resale rules in the contract — price caps, identity-bound transfers, a cut to the artist on every resale (GET Protocol).
items.alternative: A centralised platform can already cap resale prices (Ticketmaster does). The blockchain adds portability and auditability — is that worth wallets for fans?

items.title: Cross-border tuition & remittances
items.actors: International students or migrant workers · their families · banks on both sides · the university or landlord
items.friction: 3–5 days, 5–8% in fees and FX spread, no visibility on where the money is.
items.angle: Stablecoins over an L2 settle in seconds for cents; the university accepts USDC or converts on arrival (Section 3 · Borderless).
items.alternative: Fintech rails (Wise, SEPA Instant) already do this cheaply in many corridors — the case is strongest where banking access is poor.

items.title: Charity donation transparency
items.actors: Donors · the charity · field partners · auditors · regulators
items.friction: Donors can't see what happened to their money; overhead ratios are disputed; trust collapses after each scandal.
items.angle: Donations and disbursements flow through a transparent treasury contract; every payment is public; milestone-based release (DAO-style, Section 3).
items.alternative: Published audited accounts. Cheaper and legally recognised — but slower, less granular, and still based on trusting the auditor.

items.title: Carbon credit double counting
items.actors: Project developers · registries · brokers · corporate buyers · verifiers
items.friction: The same credit can be sold twice across registries; retirement is hard to prove; provenance is opaque.
items.angle: Each credit is a unique token; retiring it burns it; the full chain of custody is public (tokenised credits, Section 3 · RWA).
items.alternative: A single global registry with an API. The real problem is bad or fraudulent measurement at the source — which no ledger fixes.

items.title: Baby-formula recall
items.friction: Tracing one contaminated batch to shelves takes days; whole product lines get pulled; blame is disputed.
items.angle: Every hand-off recorded on a permissioned chain; recall scope found in seconds (Walmart Food Trust, Section 3).
items.alternative: A shared database run by the industry association. Works if everyone trusts the association — the question is whether they do.

items.title: Freelancer escrow
items.friction: Clients ghost after delivery; freelancers deliver nothing after deposit; platforms take 10–20% and freeze funds for weeks.
items.angle: Funds locked in an escrow contract; released on client approval or by a vote of arbitrators; fees fall to a few percent.
items.alternative: Existing platforms are escrow already. The contract removes the platform's discretion — and its customer support. Who settles a messy dispute?

items.title: Group-buying a rare asset
items.actors: Thousands of small contributors · an auction house · a custodian · a legal entity
items.friction: Pooling money fast across strangers is hard; deciding what happens after is harder (ConstitutionDAO, Section 3).
items.angle: A DAO treasury collects funds in days; token holders vote on custody, display, resale; exit rights protect minorities.
items.alternative: A fund or cooperative with a lawyer. Slower, but it can actually own the asset. What happens when the DAO loses the auction?

lens.heading: Should this problem earn a blockchain?
lens.subtitle: Tick what is true for your group's problem. The verdict updates live — bring it to Part 3 of your report.

checks.label: Several parties are involved who do not fully trust each other
checks.hint: If one party is trusted by all, a database wins.

checks.label: They need one shared record that no single party controls
checks.hint: Shared truth is the core thing a blockchain sells.

checks.label: The rules are simple and stable enough to write as code
checks.hint: If the policy changes monthly, immutability hurts.

checks.label: The data can be public or hashed — no raw personal data on-chain
checks.hint: GDPR and trade secrets conflict with public ledgers.

checks.label: The current intermediary is expensive, slow or a real fraud risk
Users can live with wallets — or you can hide them behind an app
checks.hint: Wallet UX is still the number-one adoption killer.

sc.title: ✅ Strong case for a smart contract
sc.desc: Multi-party, shared truth, stable rules. Your Part 3 should still name the two biggest risks — audits and governance.

hybrid.title: ⚠️ Hybrid — justify every on-chain piece
hybrid.desc: Some of the pattern fits. Most real deployments live here: hashes or ownership on-chain, data and discretion off-chain.

db.title: ❌ Probably a database
db.desc: A well-run database with audit logs is cheaper, faster and legally clearer. Saying so, with reasons, is a strong report.

lens.footnote: This is a conversation starter, not a formula. Section 4's decision tree is the full version — use both.

report.heading: The 1-page report
report.subtitle: A template you can copy. Three headings, a verdict line, your names. Nothing else.
report.pageProsConsTitle: 3 · Pros & cons of using a blockchain

submission.label: Names
submission.note: at the top of the page

strong: Names the actors and says which one is not trusted — in the first three lines.
Describes what the contract does in plain language. No code, no jargon without a gloss.
Puts data where it belongs: ownership and rules on-chain, personal data and documents off.
Gives at least two honest cons — cost, privacy, governance, user experience.
Ends with a verdict a sceptical CFO could repeat in one sentence.
Cites at least one real case from this course (success or failure) as a reference point.

discussion.prompt: Which of today's problems genuinely needs a blockchain — and which just needs a better database?
questions: Where did your group disagree most: the problem, the solution, or the verdict? What evidence would settle it?
For a ❌ verdict: what would have to change (regulation, user tools, cost) for it to become ✅?
For a ✅ verdict: who runs it, who pays the gas, and who gets blamed when it goes wrong?
Which real case from the course does your problem most resemble — Estonia, Walmart, The DAO, ASX, TradeLens, ConstitutionDAO?

rubric.heading: How it's assessed
rubric.subtitle: Four equal criteria. Critical thinking is rewarded as much as enthusiasm — a well-argued "no" scores as high as a well-argued "yes".

criteria.label: Clarity of the problem
criteria.desc: Actors, friction and today's cost are concrete. A reader knows who is not trusted and why it matters.

criteria.label: Fit of the solution
criteria.desc: The contract's trigger, action and on/off-chain split are plain and plausible. It connects to a real pattern from the course.

criteria.label: Honesty of the pros & cons
criteria.desc: Real trade-offs, not a sales pitch. The non-blockchain alternative is taken seriously. The verdict follows from the analysis.

criteria.label: Use of course concepts
criteria.desc: Decision framework, oracle problem, governance, limitations and at least one real case are used correctly — not name-dropped.

rubric.noteBody: this is one of two in-class assignments in the course. It is graded on reasoning, not on whether the answer was "blockchain".
